summary.text: Sandstone is a clastic sedimentary rock made mainly of sand-sized silicate grains, 0.0625 to 2 mm across, cemented together by another mineral.
Most sandstone is quartz or feldspar, because those minerals resist weathering at Earth's surface better than any others.
Water and other fluids usually seep through sandstone, and its pores can hold large amounts, making it valuable as an aquifer and petroleum reservoir.

facts.label: Common colors
facts.value: Tan, brown, yellow, red, grey, pink, white, black

facts.label: Famous landscape
facts.value: Red rock deserts of Arches National Park

items.prompt: After a mountain range wears down over millions of years, the sand it leaves behind is mostly one mineral. Why that one?

options.label: Quartz is the only mineral in most mountains
Weathering slowly turns other minerals into it
Quartz is hard and stable, so it outlasts the rest
Its grains are lighter, so rivers carry them away

items.explain: Quartz grains dominate because their hardness and chemical stability let them survive weathering and even repeated recycling.

items.prompt: Deep underground, buried sand grains are squeezed hardest where they touch each other. What happens at those touching points?

options.label: The strained mineral dissolves, so grains pack closer
The grains melt and fuse into glass
The grains shatter into fine silt
New crystals push the grains apart

items.explain: In pressure solution, the strained mineral at contact points is more soluble, so it dissolves away and the grains move into closer contact.

items.prompt: A town drilling for groundwater hits a thick layer of sandstone. Why is that usually good news?

options.label: It dissolves and releases fresh water
It seals water out and keeps it clean
It holds frozen water from old glaciers
Water flows through it and fills its pores

items.explain: Sandstone usually lets water percolate through and is porous enough to store large quantities, which makes it a valuable aquifer.

items.prompt: A sandstone layer gets caught in the squeeze of mountain building and undergoes metamorphism. Which rock can it turn into?

options.label: Marble
Quartzite
Slate
Granite

items.explain: Quartz-bearing sandstone can be changed into quartzite by metamorphism, usually linked to compression in mountain belts.

items.prompt: Long-buried sandstone is slowly brought back near the surface by erosion and meets rainwater again. What can happen to it?

options.label: Some cement dissolves, opening new pore space
It melts and recrystallizes into quartzite
Its grains grow several times larger
It hardens into a block of granite

items.explain: As erosion reduces burial depth, renewed exposure to meteoric water can dissolve some of the cement, creating secondary porosity.

items.prompt: Sandstone is called a clastic rock. What does that say about where its sand grains came from?

options.label: Shells of tiny sea creatures
Crystals that grew from seawater
Weathered, broken bits of older rock
Ash blown out of volcanoes

items.explain: Sandstones are clastic rather than organic or chemical: their grains come from the physical and chemical weathering of bedrock.
